title: Saving TikTok While Protecting National Security
summary:
The White House just approved a plan to keep TikTok available in the United States while adding new guardrails to address national security concerns. The order backs a sale of TikTok’s U.S. operations into a new, U.S.-based company and pauses enforcement of the app-restriction law for 120 days so the deal can be completed.

Under the plan, the new company will be majority owned and controlled by U.S. investors, with TikTok’s current parent company holding less than 20 percent. Control over the app’s code, algorithms, and content decisions will move to the new firm. Americans’ data must be stored with an American cloud provider, and independent security partners will closely monitor software updates, data flows, and any models trained on U.S. user data. The same approach will also cover Lemon8 and CapCut. The Department of Justice will not pursue penalties for past or current distribution of the app during the transition and will assert that only the federal government, not states or private parties, may enforce the law.

Who stands to benefit? The 170 million Americans who use TikTok keep access, and the many creators and small businesses that rely on it for income and advertising avoid disruption. App stores, internet hosts, and advertisers gain clarity and protection during the transition. National security officials get stronger oversight of data and software, with tighter limits on foreign control. U.S. investors and cloud providers may see opportunity as operations localize.

Who might be negatively affected? TikTok’s current parent company and some overseas investors lose control and possibly value. States and private plaintiffs looking to bring their own cases are sidelined. Rivals who expected a ban may face tougher competition. There are also risks that come with any complex handoff: technical hiccups, higher costs, and questions about how transparent and effective the new monitoring will be. Some will view the government’s expanded oversight as necessary protection; others will worry about precedent and privacy. The order leaves room for more directives if needed, so the final impact will depend on how smoothly the transition and ongoing oversight are carried out.
